title: Personal Shopping & Cooking Guide
strategy: This plan focuses on brain, heart, inflammatory, kidney-stone, metabolic, and recovery goals using source-backed personal context. Food guidance should remain patient-specific without hard-coding a first-user identity.

Carbs: None; Tier 1 uses high-fiber vegetables as the primary volume
Snacks: Seed-flour crackers such as Simple Mills

Proteins: Whole eggs, limited to 4-6 yolks per week
Veggies: Nightshades such as tomatoes, peppers, and eggplant, ideally peeled, seeded, and well-cooked
Fats and Oils: Avocado oil for high-heat cooking or roasting
Snacks: Veggie flour if not mixed with almond flour
Desserts: Non-dairy nice cream made from frozen fruit blended with unsweetened plant milk

Proteins: Fatty beef such as ribeye or brisket
Processed meats such as salami, pepperoni, or deli meats with nitrates
Snacks: Traditional crackers made with wheat and butter

chefNarrative.name: The Cold Start
chefNarrative.rule: Cook starches such as rice or potatoes a day in advance and chill them overnight. Reheating increases resistant starch and makes the meal gentler for metabolism.

chefNarrative.name: Before the Meal: The Fat Buffer
chefNarrative.rule: For a heavier Tier 3 meal such as lamb or ribeye, have the patient eat a small source of Tier 1 fat such as olive oil about 15 minutes before the meal.

chefNarrative.name: During the Meal: The Order of Operations
chefNarrative.rule: Serve fiber and protein first, then starch last. This buffers glucose response and supports brain and metabolic stability.

chefNarrative.name: The Clothe the Carbs Rule
chefNarrative.rule: Never serve starch naked. Dress rice, sourdough, or potato with a Tier 1 fat or fiber such as olive oil, avocado oil, or vegetables.

chefNarrative.name: Stone Prevention: The Citrus Squeeze
chefNarrative.rule: Keep water intake high and add fresh lemon or lime. Citrate helps inhibit calcium oxalate stone formation.
